doc.title: David Finck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 29, 2015

chapter: Sinatra and the feel of time
title: Playing ahead of or behind the beat
summary: Finck discusses leaning forward and backward in time, Ray Brown with Oscar Peterson, and Basie band figures.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Have you ever played with a singer or an instrumentalist who played so far behind the beat that you thought, “I’d better slow down?”
Not that I better slow down, but that I better make sure it doesn’t slow down. That the song doesn’t slow down. Yeah there are some guys I play with who play behind the beat, and it can be annoying.

Now is that true for drummers too? I’ve had people sort of debate about playing on top of the time, playing behind the time, and then some people say, “the time is the time.” Like if you’re on top of the time then you’re rushing.

Well I don’t know that I agree with that statement. I think that there is a way where music leans forward and leans backward. And we’re not machines. And even with a click track you can lean forward and it can be okay. And I always felt like there was some classic rhythm sections where the bass player might be a little ahead of the drummer, if you really put it up on a screen and analyzed it. And it feels unbelievable. And for whatever reason. I mean Ray Brown used to really drive hard with Oscar [Peterson] — they would rush but who cares? It was fantastic. So yeah, I don’t think there’s a rule about that. If

you listen to Basie’s band, you know certain figures, they sit back. There’s a great record of Peggy Lee singing Cy Coleman’s “I’ve Got Your Number.” And there are a couple of horn figures where you can just hear — the lead trumpet player must have said, “we’re playing it like this.” And they just play the figure just a little more relaxed than the rest of the band is. And it’s great. I mean to me that’s the music.
